exercises.approach: Pass the values and unit through `measurement_record()` to validate and store them as doubles, then call `record_mean()`.
exercises.why: The mean of 2 and 4 is 3, there are two observations, and the unit is ms, so the result is list(mean = 3, count = 2L, unit = "ms"), with every field the contract names.
exercises.wrong: Returning only `mean(values)`. A bare 3 cannot be told apart from a 3 second mean over two hundred observations, so the consumer loses both scale and sample size.

exercises.approach: Write `from_r6 <- function(x) measurement_record(x$values(), x$unit())` so the adapter uses only the Store's public methods.
exercises.why: Store keeps its data in private fields that only its methods can read. The record is a plain list holding copies of the numbers, so editing the record cannot reach back into the Store.
exercises.wrong: Reading the private environment through R6 internals. It may work today, but renaming a private field breaks the adapter, which the public methods were written to prevent.

exercises.approach: Check `S7::S7_inherits(x, Series)` first, then pass `x@values` and `x@unit` to `measurement_record()`.
exercises.why: The class check confirms which object system and class the adapter supports before any property is read, and the resulting record is identical to those from the S3, S4 and R6 adapters.
exercises.wrong: Reading `x@values` with no class check. The S4 object s4 also answers `@values`, so `from_s7(s4)` would succeed and the adapter would quietly accept a second contract.
exercises.verify: `all(vapply(records, identical, logical(1), records[[1]]))` returns TRUE, and `from_s7(s4)` stops at the class check.

exercises.approach: Require each record to state its unit, and either convert explicitly, multiplying seconds by 1000 and setting unit ms, or reject a unit the caller did not ask for.
exercises.why: unclass removes only the class attribute. Values of 2 and 4 seconds remain the numbers 2 and 4, so a caller that assumes milliseconds reads them as a thousand times smaller.
exercises.wrong: Passing `unclass(x)$values` to code that expects milliseconds. The mean of 3 is reported as 3 ms when it is really 3000 ms, and nothing warns.
exercises.verify: `unclass(x)$values` returns the same numbers as `x$values`, which shows that no conversion took place.

exercises.approach: Build the plot from data with latency 4, 7 and 9, call `ggplot2::ggplot_build(plot)$data[[1]]`, and compare its x and y columns with the input.
exercises.why: geom_point uses the identity stat, so the built layer holds the mapped values unchanged. This checks the aesthetic mapping, not how the points look on a screen.
exercises.wrong: Checking `plot$data$latency`. The input frame is stored there whatever the mapping says, so a plot with `y = time` by mistake would still pass.

exercises.approach: Build `measurement_record(numeric(0), "ms")`, call `record_mean()` and check all three fields.
exercises.why: No observations means there is no observed average, so the function returns NA_real_ explicitly, with count 0L explaining why and the unit still declared. mean of an empty vector would return NaN instead.
exercises.wrong: Reporting a mean of 0. A dashboard would show an empty period as zero latency, the best possible value, when it actually has no data.

run_note: The starter supplies values 2 and 4 with unit ms and a small `plot_data` frame of three time and latency pairs. Run it, then write one adapter per object system that returns the same plain record. When you inspect the chart in exercise 5, read coordinates through `ggplot_build()`, because the internal layout of a ggplot object is not a public contract.
checks_note: The checks confirm that each source object really belongs to its own system, S3, S4 and S7, that all four adapters produce identical records with mean 3, count 2L and unit ms, that the R6 adapter reads through public methods, that an empty record has count 0 and an NA mean, and that the built layer's x and y equal the time and latency columns. They do not check rendered pixels.
